query: What drives customer satisfaction (Overall Rating) across the different airlines?

per_column.name: cabin_crew_service_quality
per_column.rationale: Gives a qualitative axis on crew interaction (attentive/rude etc.) that adds grouping leverage beyond the numeric 'Staff Service' rating, though it partly overlaps it. Values are mostly a sound reading of the text (S1/S3/S4/S5 all match crew descriptions), but S2 asserts 'indifferent_rushed' for a review that says NOTHING about crew — an invented crew judgment, so groundedness is dented.

per_column.name: flight_operational_reliability
per_column.rationale: Delays/cancellations are a strong satisfaction driver absent from any original column, so this is a genuinely useful new axis with real variation. However groundedness is weak: in all five samples the text is silent on timing yet the value is confidently 'on_time_smooth'. Defaulting a specific positive fact onto silent rows (rather than NULL) asserts something the source does not support.

per_column.name: aircraft_condition
per_column.rationale: A distinct, useful axis (cabin/aircraft state) not captured by original ratings. Values track the text well — clean/sanitized/well-maintained -> comfortable_clean — and the column correctly uses NULL/Unknown for silent rows (large NULL count, S2 = Unknown). Minor: S2 arguably had negative aircraft cues that were dropped, but Unknown is safe, not a hallucination.

per_column.name: ground_staff_efficiency
per_column.rationale: Check-in/ground handling is a real, separate driver not in the original columns, giving useful grouping power. In every sample the text is silent on ground staff and the value is correctly 'Unknown' — appropriate abstention. Populated categories exist elsewhere in the distribution; no contradiction observed in samples.

per_column.name: problem_resolution
per_column.rationale: How complaints are handled is a meaningful, non-redundant driver. Groundedness is mostly good (S2–S5 correctly Unknown), but S1 labels a review with no problem at all as 'proactive_empathetic', reading a courtesy gesture as problem-handling — a mild over-assertion of a category the text does not warrant.

per_column.name: value_for_money_perception
per_column.rationale: Largely a categorical restatement of the existing original 'Value For Money' rating, so it adds little new analytical leverage for this query. Groundedness is also modest: none of the five sampled reviews mention price/value, yet specific verdicts like 'poor_overpriced' / 'excellent_worth_premium' are assigned by mirroring overall sentiment — asserting a value-specific claim the text does not state.

per_column.name: airline_consistency
per_column.rationale: A consistency/decline axis could help explain satisfaction trends, but it requires cross-flight/temporal evidence a single review rarely provides. Only S5 ('service was consistently good') genuinely supports its label; S1/S4 infer 'consistently_excellent' from single positive reviews, and S2 labels a clearly negative review 'standard_reliable' — assertions not grounded in the text.

judge.rationale: The added set offers several genuinely useful new axes for explaining Overall Rating that are absent from the original numeric columns — operational reliability (delays), ground staff, aircraft condition, and problem resolution — each providing a real dimension to group and compare airlines on. Two columns are weaker: value_for_money_perception is essentially redundant with the existing 'Value For Money' rating, and airline_consistency is speculative for single-review rows. Groundedness is mixed: aircraft_condition and ground_staff_efficiency read the text soundly and abstain appropriately, but flight_operational_reliability defaults 'on_time_smooth' onto silent rows, value_for_money and airline_consistency infer specific verdicts from bare sentiment, and cabin_crew/problem_resolution each show one clear over-assertion in the samples. Per the scope rule, no score reflects completeness — only the usefulness and groundedness of the columns present.
